Indian Turquoise 1957 Chrysler New Yorker With Old-School Hemi Is Pure Eye Candy
14 photos
Photo: volocars.com
Introduced in 1940 and produced through 1996, the New Yorker is Chrysler's longest-running nameplate . It's also one of the division's most iconic models. Much like the 300 letter series, the New Yorker is a desirable classic today.
As with all Mopars, I'm a big fan of the Forward Look-era New Yorker. Virgil Exner's now-iconic styling language debuted in 1955. The early design was based on his custom 1952 Imperial Parade Phaeton. The last Forward Look vehicles were produced in 1962.
The Forward Look Chryslers got their first major facelift in 1957. That's when the New Yorker gained quad headlamps and a grille that extended toward the front wheel arches. The tailfins also became significantly bigger. It's arguably my favorite of the bunch, and it's precisely why I'm showing you this 1957 drop top. This and the fact that it's an absolute gem.
The New Yorker was pretty popular for an expensive luxury car in 1957; Chrysler sold 34,620 units. However, two body styles stand out as rare. The Town & Country station wagon , for instance, was built in only 1,391 examples. The two-door convertible is even rarer, with only 1,049 units delivered. Significantly fewer of them are still around.
But rarity isn't the only thing this New Yorker can brag about. It's also one of those classics that's been restored to Concours-ready condition. The overhaul took a whopping 2,000 hours and resulted in an outstanding vehicle inside and out.
Of course, the Indian Turquoise paint and the massive amount of chrome help this land yacht stand out. The same goes for the two-tone, turquoise/white interior. This thing is pure eye candy, which isn't surprising given that the restoration cost a whopping $250,000.
If you're into shiny engine bays, this New Yorker delivers. If you ever wanted to see how a 1957 Chrysler mill looked when it rolled off the assembly line, this 392-cubic-inch (6.4-liter) V8 is exactly what you need. It's also an old-school Hemi, if you're into that.
Chrysler introduced its first Hemi engine, also known as FirePower, in 1951. Originally a 331-cubic-inch (5.4-liter) mill, the FirePower grew to 354 cubic inches (5.8 liters) in 1956. The following year, Chrysler debuted the 392-cubic-inch V8 you see here.
This engine was produced for only two model years. In addition to the New Yorker, it also powered the 300C, 300D, and the flagship Imperial line (Custom, Crown, and LeBaron). The powerplant delivered 325 horsepower in the New Yorker.
Showing only 11 miles (18 km) on the odometer (since the restoration, of course), this pristine New Yorker is up for grabs. Volo Cars is asking $144,998 to let it go. It's among the priciest examples out there. Hit the play button below for the full walkaround.
